title: Shrinking coefficients
objectives: Fit ridge regression and choose its penalty.
Read ridge as trading a little bias for a lot less variance.

screens.title: A leash on the slope
screens.prose: Twenty shares, mom against next-month return, both centred so the line passes through the origin. The slope is now $\dfrac{\sum xy}{\sum x^2 + \lambda}$, with $\sum xy = 23.0276$ and $\sum x^2 = 29.2772$. Slide $\lambda$.
screens.question: At what $\lambda$ is the slope half its value at $\lambda = 0$?

widget.label: Penalty that halves the slope
widget.accept: 29.2772 ± 1: halving needs $\sum x^2 + \lambda = 2\sum x^2$, so $\lambda = \sum x^2$.

hints.text: At $\lambda = 0$ the slope is 0.787. Find where the caption reads half of that.
The dashed line is the OLS fit; watch the solid line swing towards flat.
Half of 0.787 is 0.393. That needs the denominator doubled: $\lambda = \sum x^2 = 29.2772$.

feedback.correct: At $\lambda = 29.2772$ the denominator doubles and the slope halves.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide until the caption's slope is half the OLS slope.

byKey.half-sxx: That shrinks the slope by a third, not a half. The denominator must double.
byKey.sxy: You used $\sum xy$. The penalty adds to $\sum x^2 = 29.2772$.

explain.text: The penalty sits beside $\sum x^2$ in the denominator, so it pulls the slope towards 0 smoothly. At $\lambda = \sum x^2$ the line has half the OLS slope. No finite $\lambda$ makes it exactly flat.

screens.title: Ridge regression
screens.prose: The slope you slid is **ridge regression**. It minimises the squared misses plus a charge on the slope's size: $$\sum_i (y_i - \beta x_i)^2 + \lambda \beta^2.$$ The **penalty** $\lambda \ge 0$ sets the price of a large $\beta$.
screens.question: With $\sum xy = 23.0276$ and $\sum x^2 = 29.2772$, what is the ridge slope at $\lambda = 10$?

hints.text: Add $\lambda$ to $\sum x^2$, not to $\sum xy$.
The caption shows the slope at $\lambda = 10$.

feedback.correct: 0.586: the penalty trims the OLS slope of 0.787.

byKey.ols: That is the OLS slope, $\lambda = 0$. Add the 10 to the denominator.
byKey.minus: You subtracted the penalty. It adds to $\sum x^2$, which shrinks the slope.
byKey.top: You added the penalty on top. It belongs underneath, beside $\sum x^2$.

explain.text: $23.0276/39.2772 = 0.586$. A large slope now costs twice: in squared misses if it is wrong, in $\lambda\beta^2$ always. Ridge settles where the two costs balance.

screens.title: Where the formula comes from
screens.prose: Derive the one-feature ridge slope from the objective. Put the lines in order.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $L'(\beta) = -2\sum_i x_i(y_i - \beta x_i) + 2\lambda\beta$, differentiating term by term
$\sum_i x_iy_i = \beta\left(\sum_i x_i^2 + \lambda\right)$, setting $L'(\beta) = 0$ and dividing by 2

hints.text: Start from the quantity ridge minimises.
A minimum of a smooth function has derivative 0.
Objective, derivative, set to zero and collect $\beta$, then divide.

feedback.correct: And because $L''(\beta) = 2(\sum x_i^2 + \lambda) > 0$, it is a minimum.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write the objective, differentiate, set to zero, solve.

byKey.sol: The solution needs the equation from setting the derivative to zero first.
byKey.zero: You need the derivative before you can set it to zero.

explain.text: The only change from OLS is the $+\lambda$ beside $\sum x_i^2$. It keeps the denominator positive even when $\sum x_i^2 = 0$, which is why ridge always has an answer.

screens.title: Six coefficients shrinking
screens.prose: Now six features on 200 share-months, all z-scores, built uncorrelated so every path is a formula: each OLS coefficient times $\tfrac{200}{200 + \lambda}$. The chart shows each size $|\hat\beta_j|$. Only mom, value and vol truly matter. Slide $\lambda$.

derive.caption: $\lambda = {{lam}}$: every coefficient is {{fixed(100*200/(200 + lam), 1)}}% of its OLS value

screens.question: At $\lambda = 600$, what is mom's coefficient? Its OLS value is 0.6.

hints.text: Set $\lambda = 600$ and read the caption.
Follow the mom curve to the vertical line.

feedback.correct: 0.15: a quarter of the OLS value, and still not zero.

byKey.zero: You expected the coefficient to be gone. Ridge shrinks every coefficient but sets none to zero.
byKey.lin: You shrank it in proportion to $\lambda$. The factor is $200/(200 + \lambda)$, a curve, not a straight line.
byKey.third: You took off a quarter. Ridge keeps a quarter: $200/800$.

explain.text: Every curve shrinks by the same factor here, so the order of sizes never changes. The three noise coefficients shrink with the rest but never reach 0. Ridge trades a little bias in the real coefficients for much less noise in all of them.

screens.title: Choosing $\lambda$
screens.prose: Because we built this market, we know the exact expected test MSE at every $\lambda$: the noise, 4, plus the squared gaps between the ridge and true coefficients. Drag the point along the curve.

The curve dips just right of 0 before climbing.
The bottom is near $\lambda = 46$, where the caption reads 4.0162.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the lowest point of the curve.

byKey.ols: You stayed at OLS. A little shrinkage cuts the noise in the coefficients by more than the bias it adds.

explain.text: From $\lambda = 0$ to 46 the variance saved beats the bias added; beyond it bias wins. This is the U-shape from level 1, with $\lambda$ as the dial. In real data we do not know this curve, so we estimate it on held-out rows.

screens.title: Ridge in NumPy
screens.prose: With many features ridge solves $(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X} + \lambda\mathbf{I})\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = \mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y}$. The intercept is not penalised: centre $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{y}$ first, solve for the slopes, and the intercept is $\bar y - \bar{\mathbf{x}}^T\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$. `Ridge(alpha=lam)` does exactly this.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np

def ridge_coef(X, y, lam):
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float)
    Xc = X - X.mean(axis=0)
    yc = y - y.mean()
    p = X.shape[1]
    beta = np.linalg.solve(Xc.T @ Xc + lam * np.eye(p), Xc.T @ yc)
    return np.round(beta, 6)

widget.solution:
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error

def best_alpha(X_train, y_train, X_val, y_val, alphas):
    scores = []
    for a in alphas:
        model = Ridge(alpha=a).fit(X_train, y_train)
        scores.append(mean_squared_error(y_val, model.predict(X_val)))
    return alphas[scores.index(min(scores))]

screens.title: The two ends, and too many features
screens.prose: Back to the first lesson's 40 candidate features with only 30 training rows. OLS fitted the 30 rows exactly and tested at 23.98, against 12.15 for the training mean.
screens.question: Which statement about ridge is true?

options.text: For any $\lambda > 0$ it has one answer, even with more features than rows; $\lambda = 0$ is OLS and $\lambda \to \infty$ forecasts the training mean
It fails with more features than rows, like OLS
options.why: You carried over the OLS problem. $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X} + \lambda\mathbf{I}$ is invertible for every $\lambda > 0$.

options.text: As $\lambda \to \infty$ every forecast goes to 0%
options.why: You shrank the intercept too. Only the slopes go to 0; the intercept stays at $\bar y$, so forecasts go to the training mean.

options.text: It sets the 37 useless coefficients to 0
options.why: Ridge never sets a coefficient exactly to 0. That is the next lesson's tool.

hints.text: What happens to $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$ when $\lambda$ is added to its diagonal?
The intercept is never penalised.
$\lambda = 0$ gives OLS; huge $\lambda$ leaves only the intercept, $\bar y$; any $\lambda > 0$ gives a unique fit.

feedback.correct: Here `Ridge(alpha=30)` tests at 11.56: below the baseline's 12.15, where OLS was at 23.98.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about the two ends of $\lambda$ and the extra $\lambda$ on the diagonal.

explain.text: Adding $\lambda$ to the diagonal makes the system solvable for any shape of $\mathbf{X}$. With 30 rows and 40 features, ridge at $\lambda = 30$ tests at 11.56, about half the OLS error. At the far end it forecasts $\bar y$, the baseline itself.

screens.title: The ridge estimator
screens.prose: With $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{y}$ centred, ridge minimises $\lVert\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta\rVert^2 + \lambda\lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert^2$, and $$\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_\lambda = (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X} + \lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y}.$$ Every coefficient shrinks towards 0 and none reaches it. $\lambda$ is chosen on held-out rows.
screens.question: Why is $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X} + \lambda\mathbf{I}$ always invertible when $\lambda > 0$?

options.text: The eigenvalues of $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$ are at least 0, so adding $\lambda$ makes them all at least $\lambda > 0$
Because it is square
options.why: Square matrices can be singular: $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$ itself is square and singular with 40 features and 30 rows.

options.text: Because its diagonal is non-zero
options.why: A non-zero diagonal is not enough; $\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}$ is singular.

options.text: Because ridge drops rows until there are more rows than features
options.why: Ridge keeps every row. The fix is on the diagonal.

hints.text: Think of $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$'s eigenvalues, from the eigen course.
$\mathbf{v}^T\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v} = \lVert\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v}\rVert^2 \ge 0$.
Adding $\lambda\mathbf{I}$ adds $\lambda$ to every eigenvalue, so none is 0.

feedback.correct: Every eigenvalue moves up by $\lambda$, so none is 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the eigenvalues before and after adding $\lambda\mathbf{I}$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$ has eigenvalues $d_j \ge 0$; with $\lambda\mathbf{I}$ they become $d_j + \lambda > 0$. Small eigenvalues are where OLS coefficients explode, and that is exactly where ridge helps most.

screens.title: A 50-factor model
screens.prose: A fund's monthly return is regressed on 50 overlapping factors, with 60 months to fit. OLS gives a largest coefficient of 2.16; the truth is at most 0.4. `make_factors(seed)` builds such data. Measure how ridge reins it in.
screens.question: Complete `ridge_path(X, y, lams)` so it returns $\lVert\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_\lambda\rVert$ for each $\lambda$, each rounded to 6 places.

widget.prelude:
import numpy as np

def make_factors(seed, months=120, k=50):
    """Monthly returns (%) of k overlapping factors and of a fund that holds a little of five of them."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    common = rng.standard_normal((months, 1))
    F = 0.8 * common + 0.6 * rng.standard_normal((months, k))
    w = np.zeros(k)
    w[:5] = [0.4, 0.3, 0.2, -0.2, 0.1]
    y = F @ w + 1.0 * rng.standard_normal(months)
    return F, y

widget.solution:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge

def ridge_path(X, y, lams):
    out = []
    for lam in lams:
        coef = Ridge(alpha=lam).fit(X, y).coef_
        out.append(round(float(np.linalg.norm(coef)), 6))
    return out

explain.text: OLS spreads the fund's exposure across near-duplicate factors with huge offsetting bets, and pays for it out of sample: 13.43 against 1.60. Ridge behaves like a Bayesian prior that every exposure is probably small, the idea from the `estimation` course's Bayes lesson. The prior's strength is $\lambda$.

ideas: Ridge adds $\lambda\lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert^2$ to the squared errors, shrinking every coefficient towards 0 but never to it.
A little bias buys a lot less variance: test error against $\lambda$ is a U, and its bottom is found on a validation block.
$\lambda = 0$ is OLS, $\lambda \to \infty$ is the training mean, and any $\lambda > 0$ gives one answer even with more features than rows.

quiz.prose: `Ridge(alpha=0)` and `LinearRegression()` are fitted on the same rows.
quiz.question: How do their coefficients compare?

options.text: They are the same: with no penalty ridge is OLS
Ridge's are all 0
options.why: You mixed up the two ends. $\lambda \to \infty$ sends slopes to 0; $\lambda = 0$ leaves them at OLS.

options.text: Ridge's are a little smaller
options.why: With $\lambda = 0$ there is nothing to shrink them.

options.text: Ridge raises an error at $\lambda = 0$
options.why: It fits; the penalty term is simply 0.

explain.text: With $\lambda = 0$ the formula is the normal equations, so the coefficients match OLS.

quiz.prose: Last year a desk found $\lambda = 50$ best on returns in per cent. This year it measures returns in basis points, 100 times larger, with the same features.
quiz.question: Should it reuse $\lambda = 50$?

options.text: No: the right $\lambda$ depends on the scale of the data, so choose it again on held-out rows
Yes: $\lambda$ is a property of the model, not the data
options.why: You treated $\lambda$ as universal. It is weighed against squared errors and squared coefficients, which both depend on units.

options.text: Use $\lambda = 5{,}000$, 100 times larger
options.why: You scaled it with the target. In this setup the features did not change, so the same $\lambda$ shrinks by the same factor; but nobody should rely on such arithmetic. Re-tune it.

options.text: No: ridge cannot be used on basis points
options.why: Units do not matter to ridge's validity, only to the value of $\lambda$.

feedback.correct: A penalty is only meaningful relative to the data it is applied to.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what $\lambda$ is compared with in the objective.

explain.text: A $\lambda$ tuned on one dataset is not a number to carry across datasets with different scales, sizes or features. Treat it as something to estimate each time, on held-out rows.

quiz.prose: `Ridge` in scikit-learn centres the data and leaves the intercept out of the penalty.
quiz.question: What would go wrong if the intercept were penalised?

options.text: Forecasts would be pulled towards 0%, so shifting every return by a constant would change the fit
Nothing: the intercept is just another coefficient
options.why: You treated the average level like a feature effect. Shrinking it drags every forecast towards 0%.

options.text: The matrix would become singular
options.why: Penalising more never makes the system singular; it makes the forecasts depend on where 0 is.

options.text: The slopes would go to 0 faster
options.why: With centred data the slopes do not depend on the intercept's penalty.

feedback.correct: The average return is not a feature effect; there is no reason to shrink it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the intercept stands for.

explain.text: The intercept is the average forecast. Penalising it ties the model to an arbitrary zero point, so returns in excess of cash and raw returns would give different slopes.

quiz.prose: Uncorrelated z-scored features on $n = 300$ rows, so ridge multiplies each OLS coefficient by $n/(n + \lambda)$. An OLS coefficient is 0.45.
quiz.question: What is it at $\lambda = 150$?

byKey.half: You used $\lambda/n = 0.5$ as the factor. The factor is $n/(n + \lambda) = 2/3$.
byKey.minus: You took a third off twice. The factor is $2/3$, once.

explain.text: $300/450 = 2/3$, so $0.45 \times 2/3 = 0.30$. Half the OLS value would need $\lambda = n = 300$.
